The deployed binary self-describes. As of 0.151.0 that file says:
ThreadTokenUsageUpdatedNotification { threadId, turnId, tokenUsage },
all three REQUIRED;
ThreadTokenUsage { last, total } REQUIRED,
modelContextWindow: integer|null, OPTIONAL;
TokenUsageBreakdown { totalTokens, inputTokens, cachedInputTokens,
outputTokens, reasoningOutputTokens } REQUIRED,
cacheWriteInputTokens: integer, default 0, OPTIONAL.
There is no hermetic test of this: the check needs the codex binary, and a
test that reads an absolute path into someone's home directory would fail on
any box that is not this one. The command is documented instead, on purpose.
`cacheWriteInputTokens` is 0 in the captured frame, and is left at 0. An
earlier hand-authored version of this fixture put a non-zero number there to
'exercise the full breakdown'; the real distribution is that the key is
present in 38932 of 181344 frames on this box and was 0 in the frame taken.
The capture wins over the aesthetics.
READ THIS BEFORE USING THE NUMBERS. `total` is a LIFETIME sum over every
response in the thread; `last` is the most recent single response. This
capture makes that impossible to ignore precisely because it was not curated:
a real session ran up total.totalTokens = 65570537 against a 258400 window —
253.8x over — while last.totalTokens was 113356, about 41.1% occupancy after
the 12000-token baseline adjustment. Any code that renders ~26607% is
dividing by the wrong field. Do not 'fix' the numbers to make total smaller;
a total hundreds of times the window is what a long real thread looks like,
and this file is the evidence for it.
